## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

Finding nothing new worth a pack is a perfectly good, common outcome.

There is no windowed Context to bind — the opportunity is standing (knowledge that was never organized into a pack, not a recent change), so examine the repo as it is.

5	
6	# Generate project instructions — extract packs, not a project doc
7	
8	This skill grows the corpus's pack library using the project in front of you as the evidence, and
9	lands the project's own working rules where every project's do now: its **local packs**. The owner's
10	projects recur — not as wholes, but **along axes**: the same working style returns with a different
11	product, the same technology returns with a different working style, the same audience returns on a
12	different stack. The first project to exhibit a facet pays the cost of working out how that facet is
13	handled; a **canon** pack is how every later project sharing it starts from the answer instead of
14	re-deriving it — and what stays specific to *this* project lands in **its own local pack**, the same
15	pack machinery run from the project's tree.
16	
17	The deliverable is therefore **two kinds of pack**, never a single "how to work on this repo" document:
18	
19	- **Canon pack seeds and refinements** — one `packs/<facet>/` per facet where this project has real
20	  portable insight, each written as if this project didn't exist, proposed to Claudinite.
21	- **The project's own local pack(s)** — under `.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` in the project's tree:
22	  the project-specific working style, concrete values (real commands, paths, names, metrics), and the
23	  project-specific rules that *don't* generalize — carried the same way any pack carries them (a check
24	  in the pack's `rules`, an activity skill, prose in `RULES.md`, a scheduled task), not a thin doc.
25	  This is the project's normalized capture surface; its `CLAUDE.md` is a thin routing map to it, loaded
26	  through the pack system rather than `@import`.
27	
28	The failure mode this skill exists to prevent: investigating the repo and producing one competent "how
29	to work on this repo" document — real commands, real paths, this product's concepts — with the
30	reusable core never separated out and the project-specific core dumped as always-loaded prose. If
31	portable guidance ends up in a local pack (it should be a canon pack), or the project's file names end
32	up in a canon pack (they belong in the local pack), the split is wrong.
33	
34	## 1. Gather the evidence
35	
36	Read the project before writing a word: README and existing docs, `CLAUDE.md` and everything it
37	imports, dependency and build manifests, scripts and CI, the test layout, git history and recent
38	PRs/issues, and any conversation with the owner about how they want to work. You are collecting two
39	things, both grounded in what you actually find:
40	
41	- the **facets** this project exhibits (step 2), and
42	- every **candidate rule** — each convention, procedure, or quality bar the project works by — ready to
43	  be sorted by owner (step 3).
44	
45	Invent nothing. If a call that changes the outcome is genuinely open, ask the owner one focused
46	question (via the structured popup); otherwise take the sensible default and note it.
47	
48	## 2. Decompose into facets, and check the shelf per facet
49	
50	A project is a bundle of **facets**, each a candidate pack on its own axis:
51	
52	- **Class — the working style.** How work runs end to end: the loop by which a change is proposed,
53	  verified, and shipped; the production bar; audience and longevity. Test: the pack still fits a
54	  project on a different stack, for a different product idea.
55	- **Technology — the platform.** True for any project on that platform, whatever its class or product.
56	  Test: the pack still fits when the product and the working style change. The first project on a new
57	  platform mints its pack — an iPhone app arriving tomorrow mints `iphone-app` the same way
58	  `chrome-extension` and `aws-sam` were minted.
59	- **Aspect — a separable slice of concern**, usually with its own on-switch. `chrome-extension-release`
60	  is the same technology as `chrome-extension` at a different moment: the release/store standard a
61	  project declares only once it ships. Split an aspect out of its parent facet when its rules activate
62	  at a different time or under a different decision than the parent's.
63	- **Domain — the audience or setting**, when it changes how work is done. A children's-app pack would
64	  carry design-review, requirement-processing, and compliance rules that hold whether the app is
65	  Flutter or web; a regulated-industry pack likewise. A domain that doesn't change the working rules
66	  isn't a facet worth a pack.
67	
68	**The product itself is never a facet** — "this specific product" doesn't recur, by definition; its
69	rules land in the project's own local pack.
70	
71	And a *statement of what the product does* isn't a pack rule at all — not even a local one. A pack, canon
72	or local, homes **how we work**: the conventions, gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks
73	whatever the feature happens to be. The working-discipline rules bar the requirement-shaped rule outright;
74	here, catch it wearing a convention's clothes — a rule asserting which entities exist, what a surface must
75	render, or that a feature's parts are wired to each other. Pack-worthiness
76	is a question about the *work*, not about how load-bearing the code is — a real gap in product coverage is a
77	requirements gap, and answering it with a pack is how a feature's spec ends up somewhere nothing executes it.
78	
79	<example>
80	One extension project can exhibit four facets at once: `spec-driven-product` (class),
81	`chrome-extension` + `node` (technologies), `chrome-extension-release` (aspect, once it ships) — and
82	its local pack holds only what none of them own.
83	</example>

# Generate project instructions — extract packs, not a project doc

This skill grows the corpus's pack library using the project in front of you as the evidence, and
lands the project's own working rules where every project's do now: its **local packs**. The owner's

product, the same technology returns with a different working style, the same audience returns on a
different stack. The first project to exhibit a facet pays the cost of working out how that facet is

re-deriving it — and what stays specific to *this* project lands in **its own local pack**, the same
pack machinery run from the project's tree.

- **Canon pack seeds and refinements** — one `packs/<facet>/` per facet where this project has real

  project-specific rules that *don't* generalize — carried the same way any pack carries them (a check

to work on this repo" document — real commands, real paths, this product's concepts — with the
reusable core never separated out and the project-specific core dumped as always-loaded prose. If
portable guidance ends up in a local pack (it should be a canon pack), or the project's file names end
up in a canon pack (they belong in the local pack), the split is wrong.

imports, dependency and build manifests, scripts and CI, the test layout, git history and recent
PRs/issues, and any conversation with the owner about how they want to work. You are collecting two
things, both grounded in what you actually find:

- the **facets** this project exhibits (step 2), and
- every **candidate rule** — each convention, procedure, or quality bar the project works by — ready to
  be sorted by owner (step 3).

Invent nothing. If a call that changes the outcome is genuinely open, ask the owner one focused
question (via the structured popup); otherwise take the sensible default and note it.

A project is a bundle of **facets**, each a candidate pack on its own axis:

- **Class — the working style.** How work runs end to end: the loop by which a change is proposed,
  verified, and shipped; the production bar; audience and longevity. Test: the pack still fits a
  project on a different stack, for a different product idea.

  platform mints its pack — an iPhone app arriving tomorrow mints `iphone-app` the same way

name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:
defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash
jobs:
  claudinite-sweeps:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - name: Conformance sweep (world scope)
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs
      - name: Conformance sweep (work scope)
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/ci-work-scope.mjs --branch "${{ github.head_ref || github.ref_name }}"

  requirements-gate:
    name: Coverage gate
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - name: Every requirement leaf is claimed exactly once
        run: node dev/requirements/gate/coverage-gate.mjs

  dart:
    name: Dart packages
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # Every lane runs on Linux (decision D9). A macOS runner returns only for
    # the iOS archive-and-upload job, whose input is a build rather than a test.
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with:
          # Pinned, not "stable": a renderer change moves every golden at once,
          # which reads as the whole screen kind regressing (risk R6).

          channel: stable

        run: |
          dart pub get
          dart test
      - name: The screens, in the Flutter test renderer
        working-directory: packages/setlist_ui
        run: |
          flutter pub get
          flutter test

      - name: Every requirement, against the real screens
        working-directory: dev/requirements
        run: |
          flutter pub get
          flutter test runner_test.dart

      - name: Keep the renders that did not match
        if: failure()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: requirement-failures
          path: dev/requirements/**/failures/
          if-no-files-found: ignore

1	# Running the executable requirements
2	
3	[`requirements.md`](requirements.md) is the spec; everything here executes it.
4	The framework's conventions — layout, ids, kinds, the bijection — are the
5	`executable-requirements` pack's, so this file carries only what is specific to
6	this project.
7	
8	```
9	node dev/requirements/gate/coverage-gate.mjs          # the bijection gate
10	node dev/requirements/gate/coverage-gate.mjs --write  # regenerate the manifests and the gallery
11	flutter test runner_test.dart                         # every kind, from dev/requirements
12	```
13	
14	## The kinds
15	
16	| kind | proves | expected |
17	|---|---|---|
18	| `screen` | a rendered resting state | one golden PNG beside the case, pixel-exact, cropped to the region the leaf is about |
19	| `saga` | a multi-step story | one captioned frame per step, `<slug>.<id>.step-NN.png`, plus the generated `.captions.json` |
20	| `behavior` | a driven gesture and what it produces | coded assertions against the fakes' recordings |
21	| `logic` | a pure product rule | a coded `verify()` against shipped code |
22	
23	A case file is `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<id>.case.dart` — the slug names the
24	feature, so retitling a section never forces a rename. The folder is the kind:
25	a new way of asserting a requirement is a directory plus a registry entry in
26	[`gate/kinds.mjs`](gate/kinds.mjs). Cases reach the runner through the
27	per-kind `*_manifest.GENERATED.dart` files, which the gate writes from disk —
28	never edit one by hand.
29	
30	## The lanes
31	
32	Everything runs anywhere Flutter does, Linux included: the test renderer draws
33	and compares goldens headless, with no display server and no simulator. So a
34	change here is verified locally, in an agent session, before it reaches a pull
35	request — see the repo's own rules for the SDK install. CI runs the same
36	commands on `ubuntu-latest`.
37	
38	## What a screen case captures
39	
40	A screen case names the [`StageRegion`](../../packages/setlist_ui/lib/src/stage_region.dart)
41	its leaf is about, and the golden is that region cropped out of a full render of
42	the composed screen. The screen publishes its own region bounds through widget
43	keys, so a case asks for `.clocks` or `.jokeBody` and never for coordinates;

# Running the executable requirements

[`requirements.md`](requirements.md) is the spec; everything here executes it.
The framework's conventions — layout, ids, kinds, the bijection — are the
`executable-requirements` pack's, so this file carries only what is specific to
this project.

```
node dev/requirements/gate/coverage-gate.mjs          # the bijection gate
node dev/requirements/gate/coverage-gate.mjs --write  # regenerate the manifests and the gallery
flutter test runner_test.dart                         # every kind, from dev/requirements
```

## The kinds

| kind | proves | expected |
|---|---|---|
| `screen` | a rendered resting state | one golden PNG beside the case, pixel-exact, cropped to the region the leaf is about |
| `saga` | a multi-step story | one captioned frame per step, `<slug>.<id>.step-NN.png`, plus the generated `.captions.json` |
| `behavior` | a driven gesture and what it produces | coded assertions against the fakes' recordings |
| `logic` | a pure product rule | a coded `verify()` against shipped code |

A case file is `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<id>.case.dart` — the slug names the
feature, so retitling a section never forces a rename. The folder is the kind:
a new way of asserting a requirement is a directory plus a registry entry in
[`gate/kinds.mjs`](gate/kinds.mjs). Cases reach the runner through the
per-kind `*_manifest.GENERATED.dart` files, which the gate writes from disk —
never edit one by hand.

## The lanes

Everything runs anywhere Flutter does, Linux included: the test renderer draws
and compares goldens headless, with no display server and no simulator. So a
change here is verified locally, in an agent session, before it reaches a pull
request — see the repo's own rules for the SDK install. CI runs the same
commands on `ubuntu-latest`.

## What a screen case captures

A screen case names the [`StageRegion`](../../packages/setlist_ui/lib/src/stage_region.dart)
its leaf is about, and the golden is that region cropped out of a full render of
the composed screen. The screen publishes its own region bounds through widget
keys, so a case asks for `.clocks` or `.jokeBody` and never for coordinates;
adding a region is a case in that enum plus a key on the widget it names.

Omitting the region captures the whole screen. That is a deliberate exception —
for a leaf that claims something about the screen as a whole, like one that
compares an element against everything around it — and the case says why in a
`// whole-screen: <reason>` comment, which the gate requires. A case that
silently captured everything would still pass; it would just prove less, and
that is the failure this kind exists to avoid. Those whole-screen renders are
also what the gallery embeds at the foot of the spec, one per size class.

## Goldens

re-render with `flutter test runner_test.dart --update-goldens`, then run the
gate with `--write` so the gallery moves with them. That is never how a red case

the procedure for a mismatch (surface actual, expected and diff, ask, only then
re-baseline) is canon in the `writing-tests` skill.

When a case fails, its actual and diff renders are written to a gitignored
`failures/` directory beside the case, and CI uploads them as the
`requirement-failures` artifact.

## Determinism

Goldens are byte-compared, so every input that could move a pixel is pinned: the
SDK version in [`.flutter-version`](../../.flutter-version), the product's fonts

1	# Set list — architecture & system design
2	
3	The comedians' set-list app (working title "Set list"; repo working name
4	Claudinite) and its Cloudflare backend. Product behavior is specified by
5	[`setlist-requirements.md`](setlist-requirements.md) (the owner's screen-level
6	requirements) and illustrated by
7	[`mockups/setlist-ipad-mockups.html`](mockups/setlist-ipad-mockups.html); this
8	document is the system shape those requirements run on. The numbered executable
9	spec lives in [`../requirements/requirements.md`](../requirements/requirements.md)
10	— this doc does not duplicate requirement text.
11	
12	Owner constraints this design serves:
13	
14	1. **Ship to the app stores ASAP** — simplified, client-only flows are
15	   acceptable first.
16	2. **A backend process outside the app**: ingest a full-show recording, run
17	   segmentation + laugh detection offline/batch, and hand the comedian a link to
18	   their segmented show as a QR code.
19	3. **Cloudflare is the cloud platform.**
20	4. **iOS and Android, across phone and tablet sizes.**
21	5. **No macOS CI runner** until build artifacts are published to a store.
22	
23	## System context
24	
25	```
26	┌────────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
27	│ Flutter app (iOS,      │         │ Cloudflare                        │
28	│  Android; phone+tablet)│ upload  │  Worker API ── Workflow pipeline  │
29	│  stage mode · record   │────────▶│  R2 audio/artifacts   D1 metadata │
30	│  laugh detect · review │◀────────│  Workers AI (Whisper, embeddings, │
31	│  QR display            │ results │   LLM)   Container (ffmpeg)       │
32	└────────────────────────┘         │  share page (static assets + R2)  │
33	                                   └──────────────────────────────────┘
34	          ┌──────────────┐  HTTPS                  │
35	          │ Comedian's    │◀───────────────────────┘
36	          │ browser (QR)  │   share link: player + segmented set
37	          └──────────────┘
38	```
39	
40	Two actors: the **app user** (records their own sets live, or records a whole
41	show) and the **share recipient** (a comedian with no app, opening a QR link to
42	their already-segmented set in a browser). The share page is also the product's
43	acquisition surface — every shared set demos the product to a comedian.
44	
45	## Phasing
46	
47	Ordered by the owner's ship-ASAP constraint. Each phase is releasable on its
48	own; the build plan's tracking issue carries the step-level checkboxes.
49	
50	### Phase A — client-only MVP (store submission target)
51	
52	No backend, no accounts, everything on device. This is deliberately the
53	BitBinder-style "100% local, works offline" posture — a trust feature for
54	material-protective comedians, not just a shortcut.
55	
56	- **Set list management**: jokes as cards, set builder, the stage-mode screen
57	  from the mockups (current joke, pacing bar, countdown, 3×3 grid).
58	- **Recording**: continuous capture through the set, AAC on disk, background
59	  audio so a locked screen keeps recording.
60	- **Laugh detection, after the set**: a loudness-envelope pass over the finished
61	  recording (D7), producing timestamped events beside the audio. No classifier
62	  and no model, on device or in the cloud.
63	- **Segmentation, manual**: card taps mark bit boundaries (the mockups' "Manual
64	  switch" mode). Autodetect is explicitly out of Phase A.
65	- **Review**: per-show timeline of laugh events aligned to bit boundaries; the
66	  joke-analysis screen fed by manual boundaries + laugh events only (no
67	  transcript yet — transcript-dependent affordances stay hidden).
68	- **No transcription in Phase A.** On-device long-form ASR costs ship-speed on
69	  both platforms; transcripts arrive with the backend in Phase B.
70	
71	### Phase B — Cloudflare batch pipeline + QR share
72	
73	The owner-described backend flow: record a full show (multiple comedians or a
74	full set), upload, process offline, hand out QR links.
75	
76	- Upload from the app to R2 (presigned, direct).
77	- Pipeline (Workflow): transcribe → laugh-detect → segment → persist → publish
78	  share link.
79	- Share page in the browser: audio player streaming from R2, segmented set with
80	  laugh timeline, per-bit jump links. QR code rendered **on device** from the
81	  share URL — no server QR endpoint.
82	
83	### Phase C — the analysis product
84	
85	Cross-show joke analysis (the mockups' screen 2 at full power): takes of one
86	joke side by side, anomaly flags, room metadata queries. Autodetect-bits live
87	mode, informed by Phase B's segmentation quality. Sync of the on-device library
88	through the same backend. Designed later, on Phase B's data.
89	
90	## Client design
91	
92	One Flutter codebase for iOS and Android, phone and tablet (D1). Modules named
93	by responsibility:
94	
95	- **Library** — jokes, sets, shows; local store; everything user-deletable lives
96	  in the app's own container.
97	- **Stage** — the live screen: set list state machine (queued → live → told),
98	  countdown, pacing bar. Reads Capture's amplitude feed for the waveform strip.
99	- **Capture** — owns the recording: the platform recorder, file placement, and
100	  the monotonic clock card taps are stamped against. The only module touching
101	  the microphone.
102	- **Detect** — the loudness-envelope pass that turns a finished recording into
103	  laugh events (D7). Pure Dart over PCM: no platform API, no model, no I/O.
104	- **Review** — post-show: bit timeline, laugh alignment, take comparison.
105	- **Share** (Phase B) — upload manager (resumable, against presigned URLs),
106	  share-link list, QR rendering.
107	
108	### The platform seam
109	
110	Everything platform-specific sits behind one narrow contract, `RecordingSession`:
111	start and stop writing to a path, report seconds captured, report a current
112	amplitude, and report interruption transitions. Audio bytes never cross into
113	Dart — they go microphone → encoder → disk natively, and the file is read back
114	by Detect afterwards. What crosses the boundary is commands down and small
115	events up.
116	
117	The two implementations use each platform's high-level recorder (D10):
118	
119	| | iOS | Android |
120	|---|---|---|
121	| Recorder | `AVAudioRecorder` | `MediaRecorder` |
122	| Amplitude | metering (`averagePower`) | `getMaxAmplitude()` |
123	| Background | `audio` background mode | foreground service, microphone type |
124	| Interruption | audio-session interruption notifications | inferred (see R9) |
125	
126	Platform facts constraining this design:
127	
128	- **iOS** (verified 2026-08-20 against Apple doc JSON): App Review Guideline
129	  2.5.14 requires explicit consent and a clear recording indicator;
130	  `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` is mandatory. Audience-recording consent is a
131	  jurisdiction-law matter, not App Review — onboarding carries one line telling
132	  the comedian to observe local law and venue rules.
133	- **iOS transcription is unsuitable on-device for hour-long sets**:
134	  SFSpeechRecognizer has a ≈1-minute network limit with unreliable
135	  chunked-session timestamps
136	  ([docs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/speech/sfspeechrecognizer));
137	  [SpeechAnalyzer](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/speech/speechanalyzer)
138	  is iOS/iPadOS 26+ only. This is what puts transcription server-side (D2).
139	- **Android** (⚠ **unverified** — no authoritative source consulted yet; verify
140	  before the Android recorder is written): the microphone foreground-service
141	  type required for background capture, the API level at which it became
142	  mandatory, `MediaRecorder`'s AAC configuration, and whether an incoming call
143	  delivers an interruption callback or silently substitutes silence (R9).
144	  Play policy's equivalent of 2.5.14 is likewise unchecked.
145	
146	## Cloudflare backend design
147	
148	All limits verified 2026-08-20 against the cloudflare-docs source repo
149	(`production` branch; developers.cloudflare.com renders it).
150	
151	### Services
152	
153	- **API Worker** — small authenticated surface for the app: request upload
154	  (returns presigned R2 PUT), register show metadata, poll processing status,
155	  mint share links. Hono or plain fetch-router; no bytes flow through it
156	  (Worker request bodies cap at the plan limit, e.g. 100 MB — presigned-direct
157	  avoids the cap entirely).
158	- **R2** — `shows/` originals, `artifacts/` transcripts + laugh JSON + segment
159	  JSON, `public/` share-page audio. A 60-min 128 kbps AAC show ≈ 60 MB fits a
160	  single presigned PUT (5 GiB single-part cap); multipart only for WAV-scale
161	  files. Presigned PUTs can't enforce size — the Worker validates object size
162	  after the upload-complete callback.
163	- **Workflow `process-show`** — the pipeline orchestrator (per-step CPU to
164	  5 min, unlimited step wall-clock, results ≤1 MiB so artifacts live in R2 and
165	  steps pass keys):
166	  1. **probe** — read audio metadata, plan chunking.
167	  2. **transcribe** — time-based chunks (~1 min, cut on silence with overlap;
168	     never byte-sliced mid-frame) through `@cf/openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo`;
169	     re-offset word timestamps; stitch. Workers AI's max audio size is
170	     undocumented (Cloudflare's own tutorial chunks at 1 MB), so chunk size is
171	     a config value, found empirically. Cost ≈ $0.03/hour of audio
172	     ($0.0005/audio-min); ASR rate limit 720 req/min swallows a 60-chunk show.
173	  3. **laugh-detect** — the same loudness-envelope algorithm the client runs
174	     (D3, D7), over the full audio. Cheap enough to run in a Worker or the
175	     Container; emits laugh spans + intensity to R2.
176	  4. **segment** — bit boundaries from laughter peaks + embedding-similarity
177	     minima over the transcript (Workers AI embedding model), then an LLM pass
178	     (Workers AI) to adjudicate boundaries and name bits. The published
179	     comedy-pipeline shape (TIC-TALK; EMNLP 2021 used laughter as boundaries).
180	  5. **persist** — segments/takes/laugh stats into D1; artifacts already in R2.
181	  6. **publish** — on request, mint an unguessable share slug into D1, copy
182	     playable audio to `public/`.
183	- **ffmpeg home** — probing and chunk-cutting need ffmpeg, which Workers can't
184	  run, so a Container image carries it. That is now its only job.
185	- **D1** — `shows`, `segments`, `takes`, `laugh_events` (aggregated),
186	  `share_links`. Well under the 10 GB/db and 2 MB/row limits.
187	- **Share page** — Workers static assets (HTML/JS ≤25 MiB/file) + audio as
188	  HTTPS range requests straight from R2 (egress-free). Cloudflare Stream is
189	  explicitly not used: it rejects audio-only uploads.
190	- **Queues** — not in the v1 pipeline; the Workflow is triggered directly by
191	  the upload-complete API call. Queues enter later if fan-out (many shows at
192	  once) needs buffering.
193	
194	### Share-link flow (the QR story)
195	
196	1. Owner records a show in the app (or imports a file), uploads it.
197	2. Pipeline runs; owner reviews segments in the app, optionally trims/renames,
198	   picks the comedian's slice of the show (a show may contain several comics).
199	3. Owner taps "Share" → API mints `https://<share-domain>/s/<slug>` → app
200	   renders the QR on device → comedian scans it at the bar.
201	4. The share page needs no account: player, segmented set, laugh timeline.
202	   Slug is unguessable (128-bit); owner can revoke (row delete + `public/`
203	   object delete). A share link is the acquisition surface, so the page footer
204	   carries the store links.
205	
206	### Identity, cost, privacy posture
207	
208	- Phase A has no accounts. Phase B needs only a device-scoped API token
209	  (attestation later if abuse appears); full accounts wait until sync (Phase C).
210	- Cost at hobby scale is ~zero: Workers Paid ($5/mo) + pennies of Workers AI
211	  + R2 storage; free egress keeps share playback free.
212	- Recordings are the comedian's unreleased material — the privacy story from
213	  Phase A ("stays on your device") changes at Phase B upload, which is opt-in
214	  per show; the store privacy labels and policy change in the same release
215	  that ships upload.
216	
217	## Data model (shared vocabulary)
218	
219	- **Joke** — the durable unit of material (title, text, tags, callbacks).
220	- **Set** — an ordered list of jokes planned for a show.
221	- **Show** — one performance event (venue, time, audience descriptors) with one
222	  recording.
223	- **Segment** — a time span of a show's recording bound to a joke (manual tap
224	  in Phase A, pipeline-proposed in Phase B; provenance kept: `manual` vs
225	  `detected`, unknown stays absent, never zero).
226	- **Take** — the join of one joke across shows (what screen 2 compares).
227	- **LaughEvent** — a span of room noise: start, duration, intensity. It carries
228	  no class and no confidence, because the detector that produces it (D7) has
229	  neither to report.
230	- **ShareLink** — slug → show slice, revocable.
231	
232	## Decisions
233	
234	Numbered so review discussion can key on them; ids are stable, so a decision
235	that changes is revised in place rather than renumbered. "Recommended" = this
236	doc's call, reversible until code lands on it.
237	
238	- **D1 (recommended): one Flutter codebase, not native per platform.** The
239	  product must run on iOS and Android across phone and tablet sizes, and the
240	  platform-specific surface is now one narrow recorder contract (above) rather
241	  than a shared audio pipeline — so a second native client would duplicate the
242	  UI, the core and the requirements harness to save nothing. Flutter also keeps
243	  the executable-requirements harness on Linux, which is what makes D9
244	  reachable.
245	- **D2 (recommended): iOS 17 and Android API 26 floors; transcription
246	  server-side.** Keeps Phase A shippable broadly. On-device ASR upgrades stay
247	  opportunistic, never a floor. The Android floor is provisional until the
248	  facts above are verified.
249	- **D3 (recommended): one detector, everywhere.** The same loudness-envelope
250	  algorithm runs on device and in the Phase B pipeline, so scores are
251	  comparable by construction and no calibration pass stands between recording
252	  and cross-show analysis. A `LaughEvent` therefore names no detector; if the
253	  algorithm ever versions incompatibly, that version becomes the thing events
254	  carry.
255	- **D4 (recommended): no Cloudflare Stream, no server QR.** R2 range requests
256	  for playback; QR rendered on device.
257	- **D5 (open): share-page domain** — needs the owner's domain choice; blocks
258	  nothing until Phase B publish.
259	- **D6 (open): Whisper chunk strategy fallback** — if empirical Workers AI
260	  limits make chunk-stitching quality unacceptable, the fallback is running
261	  whisper.cpp inside a Container (CPU, batch-tolerable) or
262	  `@cf/deepgram/nova-3` ($0.0052/min). Decide on real data in Phase B.
263	- **D7 (recommended): loud is a laugh.** In a comedy club, sustained room noise
264	  above the room's own baseline is laughter; the product does not need to tell
265	  laughter from applause from cheering. Detection is therefore a loudness
266	  envelope over PCM with a threshold and a minimum duration — a pure function,
267	  no model, identical on every platform. What this buys: it is deterministic
268	  and unit-testable against a committed audio fixture, where a classifier is a
269	  platform black box that can only be trusted, never asserted.
270	- **D8 (recommended): analysis runs after the set, not during it.** Nothing
271	  classifies while the microphone is live, so capture and analysis never share
272	  a session. This removes background-classification and thermal risk outright,
273	  and it is why the platform seam can be a high-level recorder.
274	- **D9 (recommended): no macOS CI runner until store publication.** Every lane
275	  — unit, logic, behavior, screen goldens and sagas — runs on Linux, which
276	  Flutter's golden harness supports. A macOS runner returns only for the iOS
277	  archive-and-upload job, whose input is a build, not a test.
278	- **D10 (recommended): high-level platform recorders.** With no live analysis
279	  (D8) nothing needs raw PCM during capture, so `AVAudioRecorder` and
280	  `MediaRecorder` satisfy the whole contract including amplitude metering.
281	  Engine-level APIs would buy live-PCM capability the product has decided it
282	  does not want, at the cost of substantially more native code on both
283	  platforms.
284	- **D11 (recommended): one focused golden per requirement; whole-screen
285	  goldens per size class.** A leaf about one element is proved by a crop of
286	  that element at a single reference size. Only a leaf whose claim *is* the
287	  screen renders whole, and only those render once per supported size class —
288	  so the size matrix multiplies a handful of goldens, not the spec. The
289	  requirements doc owns the convention's mechanics.
290	
291	## Risks
292	
293	- **R1 — laugh detection quality on club audio.** A loudness threshold will
294	  fire on anything loud: a dropped glass, a passing siren, the PA. There is no
295	  benchmark for this on single-mic club recordings. Mitigation: Phase A ships
296	  manual segmentation regardless, so a false event costs a mark on a timeline
297	  and never a lost bit; a labeled real-set evaluation is a Phase B step, and
298	  the fix for whatever it finds lives inside one pure function.
299	- **R2 — retired.** Was: the built-in sound classifier failing while the screen
300	  is locked. Nothing classifies during capture any more (D8), so the failure
301	  mode no longer exists. Kept as an id because review discussion keys on these.
302	- **R3 — Workers AI Whisper input ceiling undocumented.** Chunk size is a
303	  config value, found empirically; D6 is the fallback.
304	- **R4 — 60-min recording thermal/battery on a phone or tablet.** Much reduced
305	  now that nothing classifies during capture, but unmeasured on real hardware.
306	  Verified by a device run, not by CI.
307	- **R5 — store review.** Recording apps clear review routinely (24–48 h
308	  typical on iOS); the consent screen, indicator (2.5.14) and truthful privacy
309	  labels are in Phase A's scope, not bolted on.
310	- **R6 — golden determinism across Flutter versions.** A renderer change shifts
311	  text rasterization and reds every golden at once. Mitigation: pin the SDK
312	  version in CI and in the environment setup, and generate and verify goldens
313	  on Linux only.
314	- **R7 — the performer's own voice dominating the envelope.** If the comedian
315	  or the PA is louder than the room, the threshold tracks the wrong signal.
316	  Mitigation: the fix lives inside Detect and changes nothing architecturally,
317	  so it is deferred deliberately until real recordings say whether it is real.
318	- **R8 — OEM battery managers force-stopping the Android foreground service**
319	  during a long set. Device-verified, not CI-verified.
320	- **R9 — Android interruption semantics.** Under the shared-microphone policy a
321	  privileged app may take the input while `MediaRecorder` keeps running and
322	  records silence, in which case no callback marks the gap and requirement 6.6
323	  must be satisfied by inference rather than by an event. Unverified; it
324	  decides how much of the Android recorder is bespoke.

          ┌──────────────┐  HTTPS                  │
          │ Comedian's    │◀───────────────────────┘
          │ browser (QR)  │   share link: player + segmented set
          └──────────────┘
```

Two actors: the **app user** (records their own sets live, or records a whole
show) and the **share recipient** (a comedian with no app, opening a QR link to
their already-segmented set in a browser). The share page is also the product's
acquisition surface — every shared set demos the product to a comedian.

## Phasing

Ordered by the owner's ship-ASAP constraint. Each phase is releasable on its
own; the build plan's tracking issue carries the step-level checkboxes.

### Phase A — client-only MVP (store submission target)

No backend, no accounts, everything on device. This is deliberately the
BitBinder-style "100% local, works offline" posture — a trust feature for
material-protective comedians, not just a shortcut.

- **Set list management**: jokes as cards, set builder, the stage-mode screen
  from the mockups (current joke, pacing bar, countdown, 3×3 grid).
- **Recording**: continuous capture through the set, AAC on disk, background
  audio so a locked screen keeps recording.
- **Laugh detection, after the set**: a loudness-envelope pass over the finished
  recording (D7), producing timestamped events beside the audio. No classifier
  and no model, on device or in the cloud.
- **Segmentation, manual**: card taps mark bit boundaries (the mockups' "Manual
  switch" mode). Autodetect is explicitly out of Phase A.
- **Review**: per-show timeline of laugh events aligned to bit boundaries; the
  joke-analysis screen fed by manual boundaries + laugh events only (no
  transcript yet — transcript-dependent affordances stay hidden).
- **No transcription in Phase A.** On-device long-form ASR costs ship-speed on
  both platforms; transcripts arrive with the backend in Phase B.

### Phase B — Cloudflare batch pipeline + QR share

The owner-described backend flow: record a full show (multiple comedians or a
full set), upload, process offline, hand out QR links.

- Upload from the app to R2 (presigned, direct).
- Pipeline (Workflow): transcribe → laugh-detect → segment → persist → publish
  share link.
- Share page in the browser: audio player streaming from R2, segmented set with
  laugh timeline, per-bit jump links. QR code rendered **on device** from the
  share URL — no server QR endpoint.

### Phase C — the analysis product

Cross-show joke analysis (the mockups' screen 2 at full power): takes of one
joke side by side, anomaly flags, room metadata queries. Autodetect-bits live
mode, informed by Phase B's segmentation quality. Sync of the on-device library
through the same backend. Designed later, on Phase B's data.

## Client design

One Flutter codebase for iOS and Android, phone and tablet (D1). Modules named
by responsibility:

- **Library** — jokes, sets, shows; local store; everything user-deletable lives
  in the app's own container.
- **Stage** — the live screen: set list state machine (queued → live → told),
  countdown, pacing bar. Reads Capture's amplitude feed for the waveform strip.
- **Capture** — owns the recording: the platform recorder, file placement, and
  the monotonic clock card taps are stamped against. The only module touching
  the microphone.
- **Detect** — the loudness-envelope pass that turns a finished recording into
  laugh events (D7). Pure Dart over PCM: no platform API, no model, no I/O.
- **Review** — post-show: bit timeline, laugh alignment, take comparison.
- **Share** (Phase B) — upload manager (resumable, against presigned URLs),
  share-link list, QR rendering.

### The platform seam

Everything platform-specific sits behind one narrow contract, `RecordingSession`:
start and stop writing to a path, report seconds captured, report a current
amplitude, and report interruption transitions. Audio bytes never cross into
Dart — they go microphone → encoder → disk natively, and the file is read back
by Detect afterwards. What crosses the boundary is commands down and small
events up.

The two implementations use each platform's high-level recorder (D10):

| | iOS | Android |
|---|---|---|
| Recorder | `AVAudioRecorder` | `MediaRecorder` |
| Amplitude | metering (`averagePower`) | `getMaxAmplitude()` |
| Background | `audio` background mode | foreground service, microphone type |
| Interruption | audio-session interruption notifications | inferred (see R9) |

Platform facts constraining this design:

- **iOS** (verified 2026-08-20 against Apple doc JSON): App Review Guideline
  2.5.14 requires explicit consent and a clear recording indicator;
  `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` is mandatory. Audience-recording consent is a
  jurisdiction-law matter, not App Review — onboarding carries one line telling
  the comedian to observe local law and venue rules.
- **iOS transcription is unsuitable on-device for hour-long sets**:
  SFSpeechRecognizer has a ≈1-minute network limit with unreliable
  chunked-session timestamps
  ([docs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/speech/sfspeechrecognizer));
  [SpeechAnalyzer](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/speech/speechanalyzer)
  is iOS/iPadOS 26+ only. This is what puts transcription server-side (D2).
- **Android** (⚠ **unverified** — no authoritative source consulted yet; verify
  before the Android recorder is written): the microphone foreground-service
  type required for background capture, the API level at which it became
  mandatory, `MediaRecorder`'s AAC configuration, and whether an incoming call
  delivers an interruption callback or silently substitutes silence (R9).
  Play policy's equivalent of 2.5.14 is likewise unchecked.

## Cloudflare backend design

All limits verified 2026-08-20 against the cloudflare-docs source repo
(`production` branch; developers.cloudflare.com renders it).

### Services

- **API Worker** — small authenticated surface for the app: request upload
  (returns presigned R2 PUT), register show metadata, poll processing status,
  mint share links. Hono or plain fetch-router; no bytes flow through it
  (Worker request bodies cap at the plan limit, e.g. 100 MB — presigned-direct
  avoids the cap entirely).
- **R2** — `shows/` originals, `artifacts/` transcripts + laugh JSON + segment
  JSON, `public/` share-page audio. A 60-min 128 kbps AAC show ≈ 60 MB fits a
  single presigned PUT (5 GiB single-part cap); multipart only for WAV-scale
  files. Presigned PUTs can't enforce size — the Worker validates object size
  after the upload-complete callback.
- **Workflow `process-show`** — the pipeline orchestrator (per-step CPU to
  5 min, unlimited step wall-clock, results ≤1 MiB so artifacts live in R2 and
  steps pass keys):
  1. **probe** — read audio metadata, plan chunking.
  2. **transcribe** — time-based chunks (~1 min, cut on silence with overlap;
     never byte-sliced mid-frame) through `@cf/openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo`;
     re-offset word timestamps; stitch. Workers AI's max audio size is
     undocumented (Cloudflare's own tutorial chunks at 1 MB), so chunk size is
     a config value, found empirically. Cost ≈ $0.03/hour of audio
     ($0.0005/audio-min); ASR rate limit 720 req/min swallows a 60-chunk show.
  3. **laugh-detect** — the same loudness-envelope algorithm the client runs
     (D3, D7), over the full audio. Cheap enough to run in a Worker or the
     Container; emits laugh spans + intensity to R2.
  4. **segment** — bit boundaries from laughter peaks + embedding-similarity
     minima over the transcript (Workers AI embedding model), then an LLM pass
     (Workers AI) to adjudicate boundaries and name bits. The published
     comedy-pipeline shape (TIC-TALK; EMNLP 2021 used laughter as boundaries).
  5. **persist** — segments/takes/laugh stats into D1; artifacts already in R2.
  6. **publish** — on request, mint an unguessable share slug into D1, copy
     playable audio to `public/`.
- **ffmpeg home** — probing and chunk-cutting need ffmpeg, which Workers can't
  run, so a Container image carries it. That is now its only job.
- **D1** — `shows`, `segments`, `takes`, `laugh_events` (aggregated),
  `share_links`. Well under the 10 GB/db and 2 MB/row limits.
- **Share page** — Workers static assets (HTML/JS ≤25 MiB/file) + audio as
  HTTPS range requests straight from R2 (egress-free). Cloudflare Stream is
  explicitly not used: it rejects audio-only uploads.
- **Queues** — not in the v1 pipeline; the Workflow is triggered directly by
  the upload-complete API call. Queues enter later if fan-out (many shows at
  once) needs buffering.

### Share-link flow (the QR story)

1. Owner records a show in the app (or imports a file), uploads it.
2. Pipeline runs; owner reviews segments in the app, optionally trims/renames,
   picks the comedian's slice of the show (a show may contain several comics).
3. Owner taps "Share" → API mints `https://<share-domain>/s/<slug>` → app
   renders the QR on device → comedian scans it at the bar.
4. The share page needs no account: player, segmented set, laugh timeline.
   Slug is unguessable (128-bit); owner can revoke (row delete + `public/`
   object delete). A share link is the acquisition surface, so the page footer
   carries the store links.

### Identity, cost, privacy posture

- Phase A has no accounts. Phase B needs only a device-scoped API token
  (attestation later if abuse appears); full accounts wait until sync (Phase C).
- Cost at hobby scale is ~zero: Workers Paid ($5/mo) + pennies of Workers AI
  + R2 storage; free egress keeps share playback free.
- Recordings are the comedian's unreleased material — the privacy story from
  Phase A ("stays on your device") changes at Phase B upload, which is opt-in
  per show; the store privacy labels and policy change in the same release
  that ships upload.

## Data model (shared vocabulary)

- **Joke** — the durable unit of material (title, text, tags, callbacks).
- **Set** — an ordered list of jokes planned for a show.
- **Show** — one performance event (venue, time, audience descriptors) with one
  recording.
- **Segment** — a time span of a show's recording bound to a joke (manual tap
  in Phase A, pipeline-proposed in Phase B; provenance kept: `manual` vs
  `detected`, unknown stays absent, never zero).
- **Take** — the join of one joke across shows (what screen 2 compares).
- **LaughEvent** — a span of room noise: start, duration, intensity. It carries
  no class and no confidence, because the detector that produces it (D7) has
  neither to report.
- **ShareLink** — slug → show slice, revocable.

## Decisions

Numbered so review discussion can key on them; ids are stable, so a decision
that changes is revised in place rather than renumbered. "Recommended" = this
doc's call, reversible until code lands on it.

- **D1 (recommended): one Flutter codebase, not native per platform.** The
  product must run on iOS and Android across phone and tablet sizes, and the
  platform-specific surface is now one narrow recorder contract (above) rather
  than a shared audio pipeline — so a second native client would duplicate the
  UI, the core and the requirements harness to save nothing. Flutter also keeps
  the executable-requirements harness on Linux, which is what makes D9
  reachable.
- **D2 (recommended): iOS 17 and Android API 26 floors; transcription
  server-side.** Keeps Phase A shippable broadly. On-device ASR upgrades stay
  opportunistic, never a floor. The Android floor is provisional until the
  facts above are verified.
- **D3 (recommended): one detector, everywhere.** The same loudness-envelope
  algorithm runs on device and in the Phase B pipeline, so scores are
  comparable by construction and no calibration pass stands between recording
  and cross-show analysis. A `LaughEvent` therefore names no detector; if the
  algorithm ever versions incompatibly, that version becomes the thing events
  carry.
- **D4 (recommended): no Cloudflare Stream, no server QR.** R2 range requests
  for playback; QR rendered on device.
- **D5 (open): share-page domain** — needs the owner's domain choice; blocks
  nothing until Phase B publish.
- **D6 (open): Whisper chunk strategy fallback** — if empirical Workers AI
  limits make chunk-stitching quality unacceptable, the fallback is running
  whisper.cpp inside a Container (CPU, batch-tolerable) or
  `@cf/deepgram/nova-3` ($0.0052/min). Decide on real data in Phase B.
- **D7 (recommended): loud is a laugh.** In a comedy club, sustained room noise
  above the room's own baseline is laughter; the product does not need to tell
  laughter from applause from cheering. Detection is therefore a loudness
  envelope over PCM with a threshold and a minimum duration — a pure function,
  no model, identical on every platform. What this buys: it is deterministic
  and unit-testable against a committed audio fixture, where a classifier is a
  platform black box that can only be trusted, never asserted.
- **D8 (recommended): analysis runs after the set, not during it.** Nothing
  classifies while the microphone is live, so capture and analysis never share
  a session. This removes background-classification and thermal risk outright,
  and it is why the platform seam can be a high-level recorder.
- **D9 (recommended): no macOS CI runner until store publication.** Every lane
  — unit, logic, behavior, screen goldens and sagas — runs on Linux, which
  Flutter's golden harness supports. A macOS runner returns only for the iOS
  archive-and-upload job, whose input is a build, not a test.
- **D10 (recommended): high-level platform recorders.** With no live analysis
  (D8) nothing needs raw PCM during capture, so `AVAudioRecorder` and
  `MediaRecorder` satisfy the whole contract including amplitude metering.
  Engine-level APIs would buy live-PCM capability the product has decided it
  does not want, at the cost of substantially more native code on both
  platforms.
- **D11 (recommended): one focused golden per requirement; whole-screen
  goldens per size class.** A leaf about one element is proved by a crop of
  that element at a single reference size. Only a leaf whose claim *is* the
  screen renders whole, and only those render once per supported size class —
  so the size matrix multiplies a handful of goldens, not the spec. The
  requirements doc owns the convention's mechanics.

## Risks

- **R1 — laugh detection quality on club audio.** A loudness threshold will
  fire on anything loud: a dropped glass, a passing siren, the PA. There is no
  benchmark for this on single-mic club recordings. Mitigation: Phase A ships
  manual segmentation regardless, so a false event costs a mark on a timeline
  and never a lost bit; a labeled real-set evaluation is a Phase B step, and
  the fix for whatever it finds lives inside one pure function.
- **R2 — retired.** Was: the built-in sound classifier failing while the screen
  is locked. Nothing classifies during capture any more (D8), so the failure
  mode no longer exists. Kept as an id because review discussion keys on these.
- **R3 — Workers AI Whisper input ceiling undocumented.** Chunk size is a
  config value, found empirically; D6 is the fallback.
- **R4 — 60-min recording thermal/battery on a phone or tablet.** Much reduced
  now that nothing classifies during capture, but unmeasured on real hardware.
  Verified by a device run, not by CI.
- **R5 — store review.** Recording apps clear review routinely (24–48 h
  typical on iOS); the consent screen, indicator (2.5.14) and truthful privacy
  labels are in Phase A's scope, not bolted on.
- **R6 — golden determinism across Flutter versions.** A renderer change shifts
  text rasterization and reds every golden at once. Mitigation: pin the SDK
  version in CI and in the environment setup, and generate and verify goldens
  on Linux only.
- **R7 — the performer's own voice dominating the envelope.** If the comedian
  or the PA is louder than the room, the threshold tracks the wrong signal.
  Mitigation: the fix lives inside Detect and changes nothing architecturally,
  so it is deferred deliberately until real recordings say whether it is real.
- **R8 — OEM battery managers force-stopping the Android foreground service**
  during a long set. Device-verified, not CI-verified.
- **R9 — Android interruption semantics.** Under the shared-microphone policy a
  privileged app may take the input while `MediaRecorder` keeps running and
  records silence, in which case no callback marks the gap and requirement 6.6
  must be satisfied by inference rather than by an event. Unverified; it
  decides how much of the Android recorder is bespoke.

20	        FlutterMethodChannel(name: Self.methodChannel, binaryMessenger: registrar.messenger())
21	            .setMethodCallHandler { [weak self] call, result in
22	                self?.handle(call, result: result)
23	            }

25	            .setStreamHandler(self)

30	            name: AVAudioSession.interruptionNotification,
31	            object: AVAudioSession.sharedInstance()

35	    private func handle(_ call: FlutterMethodCall, result: @escaping FlutterResult) {
36	        switch call.method {
37	        case "start":
38	            guard let path = (call.arguments as? [String: Any])?["path"] as? String else {
39	                result(FlutterError(code: "no-path", message: "start needs a path", details: nil))
40	                return
41	            }
42	            do {
43	                try start(atPath: path)
44	                result(nil)
45	            } catch {
46	                result(FlutterError(code: "start-failed", message: "\(error)", details: nil))
47	            }
48	        case "stop":
49	            stop()
50	            result(nil)

52	            result(FlutterMethodNotImplemented)
53	        }
54	    }

56	    private func start(atPath path: String) throws {
57	        let url = URL(fileURLWithPath: path)
58	        try FileManager.default.createDirectory(
59	            at: url.deletingLastPathComponent(),
60	            withIntermediateDirectories: true
61	        )
62	
63	        let session = AVAudioSession.sharedInstance()
64	        // `.record` with the background-audio entitlement is what keeps capture
65	        // alive behind a locked screen (requirement 6.5).
66	        try session.setCategory(.record, mode: .default)
67	        try session.setActive(true)
68	
69	        let recorder = try AVAudioRecorder(url: url, settings: [
70	            AVFormatIDKey: kAudioFormatMPEG4AAC,
71	            AVSampleRateKey: 44_100,
72	            AVNumberOfChannelsKey: 1,
73	            AVEncoderBitRateKey: 128_000,
74	        ])

97	                "level": max(0, (recorder.averagePower(forChannel: 0) + 50) / 50),

114	            sink?(["type": "resumed", "captured": recorder?.currentTime ?? 0])

116	            break

52	    }

2:
3:The numbered spec for the Set list app: what each surface must render, how it
4:must behave, the exact copy it carries. Every leaf — a numbered line
5:with no finer-numbered child — is claimed by **exactly one** case under this
6:directory, and the picture under a leaf **is** its expected rendering.
7:

10:owner's screen-level requirements in
11:[`../design/setlist-requirements.md`](../design/setlist-requirements.md) and
12:the mockups in
13:[`../design/mockups/setlist-ipad-mockups.html`](../design/mockups/setlist-ipad-mockups.html).
14:Phase B (backend pipeline, QR share) and Phase C (cross-show analysis,
15:autodetect) add their own sections when they are built.
16:

18:
19:The feature-level story — what the product is and why — lives in the design
20:docs above; this document holds only statements a case can prove. The
21:framework (kinds, runners, goldens, the coverage gate, how to add or change a
22:requirement) is in [README.md](README.md).
23:
24:**Numbering.** Every leaf carries a stable id. Add new requirements under new
25:numbers; never renumber or reuse a retired one — the ids are what cases,
26:commits and review discussion key on.
27:

29:resting state, pixel-exact against a committed golden. `saga` — a multi-step
30:story, captured as one captioned frame per step. `behavior` — a driven
31:gesture and the consequence it produces, asserted in code against the fakes'
32:recordings. `logic` — a pure product rule proved against shipped code. Each
33:case file is `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<id>.case.swift`, the slug naming the
34:feature so retitling a section never forces a rename.
35:
36:**The picture is the smallest surface that proves its leaf.** A leaf about one
37:element is proved by a picture of that element, cropped out of a full render of
38:the composed screen — never by laying the element out on its own, which would
39:prove it in a context the product never shows. Reviewing a spec means looking at
40:what each line claims, and a reader asked to re-read a whole screen for every
41:line stops reading. A whole-screen picture is a deliberate exception, for a leaf
42:that really is about the whole screen, and its case says so in a
43:`// whole-screen:` comment the coverage gate demands.
44:
45:**Whole-screen renders live at the foot of the document**, under
46:[Full-screen renders](#full-screen-renders); their leaves carry a generated link
47:there instead of a page-tall image. Everything else renders inline, cropped, at
48:one reference size. That keeps the numbered spine scannable: a reader skims the
49:claims, and goes to the bottom when they want to see a whole screen.
